newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Oct 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Oct 27.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
SUNDAY TELEGRAPH
-- MANSER LANDS TOP JOB DESPITE SCANDAL

Chief executive of securities house Robert Fleming, John Manser, is set to be promoted to chairman. The decision is yet to be ratified by the board but Manser is the choice of the Fleming family, who speak for 35 percent of the shares. Insiders say the Fleming family has put a price tag of 20 stg a share on the firm.
-- TRUST FIRMS PIN THEIR HOPES ON VOLUNTARY CODE

In an attempt to escape rule changes or legislation in the wake of the Morgen Grenfell scandal, the unit trust industry will publish a voluntary code of conduct. The code will be unveiled by the executive of the Association of Unit Trusts and Investment Funds. The rules the code is designed to reinforce relate to the holding of pre-listed securities by unit trust fund managers.
-- TELEWEST TO GO NATIONAL

The country's largest quoted cable group, Telewest, is to go ahead with plans to build its own national telecoms network in the wake of the recent deal by Cable and Wireless. The move will cost Telewest 100 million stg and will transform the business from a regional cable company with seven franchises, into a national broadband carrier, capable of carrying voice, data and video.
-- CLASH OF SYMBOLS SINK THE GAS GOLDFISH

British Gas is having problems with the name and design of its Goldfish credit card, which could cost the company 30 million stg. The design consultancy Addison has launched legal action against the group, which uses the goldfish design as its logo. Addison will see British Gas in the High Court early next year.
-- HEDGE FUND SEEKS 100 MILLION DOLLARS

SBC Warburg WSG.L is set to float on the first London- listed hedge fund in a retail and institutional share offer with the hope of raising 100 million dollars. The fund will buy into existing hedge funds, including the Quantum funds run by George Soros and not run its own investments.
SUNDAY TIMES
-- MERCURY NAME TO DISAPPEAR AFTER CABLE AND WIRELESS
MERGER

The name of Mercury Communications is set to disappear following the four-way merger announced by Cable and Wireless. Chief executive of C&W Dick Brown plans to drop the logo and establish C&W as the second telecoms and multi-media brand in Britain. Mercury will become part of the new company with the working title of Cable and Wireless Communications.
-- ROLLS STRIPS DOWN TO AEROSPACE

Rolls-Royce is planning a reorganisation which will mean the sale of many of its remaining industrial power operations along with its materials-handling business. Chief executive John Rose wants to focus resources on the company's aerospace operations and on its aero-derived industrial power business, along with its specialised nuclear business.
-- MOD OPENS THE WAY FOR A BAE -GEC LINK

The Ministry of Defence is set to drop its opposition to a defence-equipment alliance between British Aerospace and GEC. This will renew speculation about an eventual deal between the two. Insiders say BAe is ready to countenance a deal because of a series of recent developments, including the accelerating pace of restructuring in the world defence industry.
-- HOW MIDDLETON MISSED HARDING DEATH CRASH

Chief executive of Salomon Brother's European operations, Peter Middleton, changed his mind about going in the helicopter hired by Chelsea football club vice-chairman Matthew Harding. Middleton now insists he will never travel by helicopter again. Middleton's life was saved by a committment to speak at a meeting of graduates from a business school.
-- SAINSBURY SET TO LOSE PROFIT LEAD

Supermarket group Sainsbury is on a path to losing its position as Britain's most profitable grocer after dismal interim results. The City expects the group to report its worst fall in interim profit, a drop of up to 15 percent. The plunge comes from the group's core supermarket chain, which has seen profit margins suffer in a fresh outbreak of price cutting.
THE OBSERVER
-- BASS BREWS UP PLAN TO SELL 200 PUBS

Bass, the brewing group, is in talks with the intention to sell hundreds of outlets of pub entrepreneur Michael Cannon. The future of 200 pubs now hangs on the outcome. Bass could be helped by giving up outlets to allay the fears of competition authorities over the company's plans to buy Allied Domecq's half share in Carlsberg-Tetley.
-- EDDIE'S RIGHT OVER RATE RISE, SAY MOST CITY ECONOMISTS

According to a survey carried out for the Observer by financial news agency Market News, most City economists believe interest rates should rise to keep the lid on inflation. None expected Chancellor Kenneth Clarke to bow to pressure from Bank of England Governor Eddie George, for an increase at their monthly monetary meeting on Wednesday.
-- BIDDING PUSHES WILLIAMS SELL-OFF PRICE TO 350
MILLION STG

The international industrial group Williams Holdings is set to raise 350 million stg by selling some of its building products businesses, including Rawlplug, Swish curtain rails and Valor gas fires, to one of three venture capital firms; CVC Capital Partners, Canover and BCP.
-- SMALL SAVERS SET TO GAIN 1,000 STG ALLIED AND LEICESTER
WINDFALL

When the building society Allied and Leicester joins the stock market next year millions of savers and borrowers are in line for payments of 1,000 stg each. A&L will announce that it will give equal amounts of shares to all eligible members. A&L is expected to be worth 2.5 billion stg on the stockmarket.
-- PROTON TAKES THE WHEEL AT LOTUS

Lotus, the British motoring legend, is set to be sold to Proton, the Malaysian carmaker, which will produce the sports car at its plant in Kuala Lumpur. Proton offered 52 million stg for an 80 percent stake and agreed to absorb 12 million stg in debt. Proton won the deal after pledging to continue manufacturing at Lotus' base at Hethel, Norfolk, and to allow owner Romano Artioli to keep a 20 percent stake.
INDEPENDENT ON SUNDAY
-- NEW TORIES IN BUSINESS LOBBY

An analysis by the Public Policy Unit of new Tory candidates in safe seats shows that Conservative Party links with business lobbyists are set to be strengthened after the next election, with a quarter of the new 60-plus Tory intake having a consultancy or public relations background. Sixteen prospective Tory MPs who work for political lobbyists describe themselves as public affairs consultants or are known to work in the public relations industry.
-- BOEING POACHES ENGINEERS

Aircraft maker Boeing has responded to a shortage of skills in the US by launching a Europe-wide offer of six-figure dollar salaries with the aim of poaching more than 1,500 highly qualified engineers from Britain to help build its next generation of aircraft. Senior vice-president of TAD Technical Services, Tony Docherty, has been hired to find 3,000 engineers.
-- FACIA FACING LIQUIDATION

The collapsed retailer run by Stephen Hinchliffe, Facia, is set to go into liquidation with the appointment of accountants Stoy Hayward. The payout is expected to be between 700,000 stg and 5.6 million stg. Stoy Hayward is the choice of retail giant Sears for the liquidation of all the Facia companies, against which it has lodged a 30 million stg claim.
-- ZENECA'S ONE BILLION DOLLAR BLOCKBUSTERS

The pharmaceutical company Zeneca is set to bring two new products to market which have the potential to generate sales of up to one billion dollars a year: Accolate, the oral treatment for asthma and the first drug which has been developed purely in the US and Amistar, and a new fungicide.
-- AIR FRANCE SEEKS VIRGIN HELP TO BLOCK BA

In a last-ditch attempt to scupper British Airway's plans to acquire the private French airline which is in the hands of administrators, Air Liberte, Air France has invited Virgin Express to join a consortium bid. However, if Air France does not put the bid together quickly administrators will hand control of Air Liberte to BA.
MAIL ON SUNDAY
-- TRAGEDY SHAKES LLOYD'S

The death of the vice-chairman of the Chelsea Football Club, Matthew Harding, has lead to a shakeout at Lloyd's insurance market. The Benfield Group, which is at the heart of the Harding empire, is a dominant reinsurance broker specialising in laying-off risks for underwriters at Lloyd's. Lloyd's underwriters are now considering whether to continue using Benfield to buy reinsurance for them.
-- NODDY MAY BE OFF TO TESCO

Trocadero, the leisure group, is talking to several High Street chains, including Marks and Spencer, Safeway and Tesco, about licencing its Noddy and Big Ears characters. A deal will let the supermarkets promote clothes, toys and books. Trocadero will earn royalties from product sales.
-- US SHOE GIANT TO STEP IN

Nine West, a leading US shoe retailer, is close to finalising the purchase of a small British company that is in administration, Pied a Terre. Nine West is also talking to several other potential acquisitions among shoe chains in the UK and Europe.
-- CHARLES, KING OF INVESTMENT

A new book by James Morton, called 'Investing with the Grand Masters' devotes a chapter to Prince Charles, saying he has become a top fund manager by creating more entrepreneurs and successfully backing more start-ups than anyone else. The Prince's Youth Business Trust is lauded as the largest non- government new business agency in Britain.
